4856-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
Discord inside the Dutch camp fills this 1588 volume, and John Lothrop Motley follows the feuds that weakened the republic even as Spain threatened France. Leicester's resignation arrives, Willoughby and Maurice trade enmity, and the States clash with Leicester's supporters while Sonoy's rebellion comes to an end.

Across the Channel, Philip stirs civil war in France, the Catholic League threatens Henry, and a Spanish agent is welcomed in Paris as the king flees. Dutch church deputies then present long memorials to Elizabeth, pleading for steadier support. Motley shows a republic arguing with itself and its protector, while its enemy exploited division abroad.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-1588b:
The second part of chapter eighteen in John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands brings Leicester's resignation to Holland. Dangerous discord rules North Holland in the winter of 1588. Elizabeth and Burghley still cling to their delusion of a separate peace. Leicester's intrigues, Motley charges, had done much to paralyze the republic.

His departure without laying down his authority gave the signal for civil war. Meanwhile the Duke of Parma prepares in Flanders to cooperate with the armaments from Spain. A combined movement might still destroy his whole plan, Motley argues. The chapters count the cost of faction while the Armada gathers. Barneveld and the States must hold a divided country together. It is history written as a warning about allies, favourites, and delay.
uslaw-usc-t2-s168b:
Section 168b of Title 2 of the United States Code orders extra copies of a famous reference book. The book is the Constitution Annotated, the revised hardbound editions prepared under section 168. Its pocket-part supplements, which keep it current, are included in the print run.

The number of additional copies is fixed at four thousand eight hundred and seventy. The copies are divided among three users by name. Two thousand six hundred and thirty-four go to the House of Representatives. One thousand two hundred and thirty-six go to the Senate. One thousand go to the Joint Committee on Printing. The section goes on to name further recipients, beginning with all Members of Congress and the Vice President. It is a distribution list for the government's own guide to its Constitution.
uslaw-usc-t2-s288b:
Section 288b of Title 2 sets the gates for the Senate Legal Counsel's work in court. The Counsel defends the Senate, or a committee, Member, officer, or employee of it, only when directed. The direction must come from two-thirds of the Members of the Joint Leadership Group, or from a resolution adopted by the Senate.

A civil action to enforce a Senate subpoena needs the second kind of direction. Only a resolution of the Senate can start it. Intervention in a case, or appearance as a friend of the court, in the name of the Senate likewise needs a Senate resolution. The Counsel thus acts as an instrument of the whole body, not on private instruction. The section sits in Chapter 9D of Title 2, on the Office of Senate Legal Counsel. The hosted Code is current through Public Law 119-134.
uslaw-usc-t2-s28b:
Section 28b of Title 2 orders the printing of the Precedents of the House of Representatives as a public document. Two thousand sets are to be printed and bound. The Precedents are the work compiled and prepared by Lewis Deschler. They were prepared under an appropriation act named in the text.

The number of sets authorized by this group of sections replaces the usual number. It stands in lieu of the copies for binding and distribution that a provision of Title 44 would otherwise require. The sections that follow in the same range govern the sets further. The section sits in Chapter 2 of Title 2, on the organization of Congress. The hosted Code text is published by the Office of the Law Revision Counsel, current through Public Law 119-134. Print, in this corner of the Code, is still how precedent is preserved and spread.
uslaw-usc-t2-s658b:
Section 658b of Title 2 of the United States Code sets the duties of panels of Congress on mandates. It sits in Chapter 17A, on the budget and the money work of Congress, in a part on federal mandates. When a panel of the Senate or of the House reports a bill of a public kind, a rule holds. The bill or joint resolution in view must hold a federal mandate. The report of the panel that goes with the bill must then hold a set of facts.

Those facts are the ones called for by two named parts of the section. A second clause deals with the send of bills to a named man. When a panel gives the order to report such a bill, the panel is to give the bill at once to the Director of the Congressional Budget Office.
